claims.text: A visitor guide notes that although the noodles are 100% buckwheat, "soy sauce in Japan these days is not entirely wheat-free," and recommends confirming the exact ingredients with the restaurant before dining if celiac disease is a concern.

The shop's tsuyu is built from a kaeshi made with soy sauce, mirin, and sugar, aged in buried earthen pots for about a week before being combined with the dashi — this is standard shoyu, not a wheat-free formulation.

The dashi used for both the cold dipping sauce and hot noodle broths is made from hon-karebushi, a deeply cured, mold-ripened bonito, simmered fresh each morning for about 90 minutes — meaning the standard tsuyu used across the menu is fish-based.
The soba itself is juwari (十割) — cut from 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat flour used as a binder, and the buckwheat is milled fresh each day rather than pre-ground and stored.

name: 煮干中華そば 鈴蘭 (Niboshi Chuka Soba Suzuran)

claims.text: No allergen or gluten-free accommodations were found in any source; this is a conventional wheat-noodle ramen shop where cross-contact with wheat is presumed throughout (shared broth pots, shared noodle-boiling water, shoyu-based tare).
The shop's ramen and tsukemen use a shoyu/tare-seasoned niboshi-tonkotsu-chicken soup, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce was mentioned.
The signature soup is a triple stock of pork bone (tonkotsu), chicken, and dried sardine (niboshi), with no vegetarian or vegan broth option mentioned anywhere.

name: 農家の台所 新宿三丁目店 (Nouka no Daidokoro (Shinjuku Sanchome))

claims.text: The salad-bar dressing is described as a miso-type dressing (with salt, olive oil, vinegar); miso is frequently produced with barley (mugi) or wheat koji, i.e. a hidden gluten source on the shared bar that no GF claim addresses.
claims.source: https://rocketnews24.com/2024/07/22/2314665/ (via web search summary; also tabelog matome)

claims.text: A critical review notes there is no ingredient labeling on the salad-bar dishes and expresses doubt about the dressing/seasoning components (and possible excess sugar).

No celiac-specific reviews, cross-contamination protocols, or GF certification could be found on FindMeGlutenFree or HappyCow for this restaurant; only a generic 'rice flour batter so celiacs can enjoy' marketing-style statement appears, which ignores shared-fryer and wheat-soy-sauce risk.
The shop's own site and the WE TABLE aggregator page (which supplies the GF tag) returned HTTP 403 egress-policy denials and could not be read, so the claimed GF accommodation remains unverified.
The miso soup included in lunch sets is made with fish dashi, but it can be requested to be left off the set when ordering.
Only the curry among the lunch set options is vegan-compatible.
All toppings on the salad bar use no animal-derived ingredients, so vegan diners can eat freely from the salad bar alone.
Tagged on WE TABLE as accommodating allergy, vegan, halal, and gluten-free needs.

name: オーガニックごはん かえもん 浅草本店 (Organic Gohan Kaemon Asakusa Honten)

claims.text: The kitchen does not prepare meat, fish, egg, or dairy dishes at all — it is a fully plant-based operation, and miso soup/broths reportedly use a vegetable-scrap broth ("vege broth") instead of bonito-based dashi.

Restaurant explicitly markets itself as "food barrier-free," avoiding meat, fish, egg, dairy, and the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, scallion, Chinese chive, shallot) so that diners with a range of dietary and religious restrictions can eat there.
Listed on Vegewel's curated directory of vegetarian/vegan/gluten-free-friendly restaurants near Asakusa Station.

name: PAMOJA (コーヒーとおにぎり PAMOJA 神保町本店)

claims.text: No gluten-free protocol; the only GF mention is an aggregator tag on Vegewel (「グルテンフリーメニューあり」), not a venue claim. Rice base is naturally GF but fillings and shared soy sauce are the risk.
Multiple fillings are soy-sauce-simmered tsukudani/nimono (生姜昆布, まぐろ昆布, アサリの佃煮, いわしの生姜煮) — wheat risk unless tamari is used.
Standard soy sauce (wheat) appears across simmered fillings, okaka, and teriyaki tofu; no statement that tamari is used. Must confirm per item.
Mixed kitchen handling fish and meat onigiri (塩サバ, 旨味サケ, 生たらこ, 肉味噌) alongside vegan items — shared rice-pressing station is a cross-contact consideration for strict vegans.
No published allergy-handling procedure; hours and service are irregular and directed to Instagram. Treat as ask-and-verify in person.
Rice-based menu with organic ingredients and a documented vegan lineup, giving a naturally low-gluten baseline if fillings are chosen carefully.
Plain-salt fish onigiri (塩サバ, 旨味サケ) are the most likely wheat-free choices for a celiac to confirm.

name: フォーハノイ屋台33 ルミネエスト新宿店 (Pho Hanoi Yatai 33 Lumine Est Shinjuku)

claims.text: 特製スープは鶏ガラと豚骨、玉ねぎ、生姜、ベトナム調味料を長時間煮込んで旨味を抽出したもの — the house broth is chicken bone AND pork bone simmered with onion, ginger and Vietnamese seasonings, i.e. a shared animal-based stock; no meat-free vegan broth is documented.

各フォーメニューにはハーフの生春巻き、揚げパン、追い野菜、小さなデザートが付きます — every pho set is served with a half fresh spring roll, deep-fried wheat bread (揚げパン), extra vegetables and a small dessert, placing fried wheat and a spring roll on the celiac's own dish by default.

Menu confirmed to include banh mi, 生春巻き (fresh spring rolls) and fried items produced in the same kitchen; no gluten-free, allergen, dedicated-fryer, or wheat-free seasoning statement found on the shop site or any listing.

General Vietnamese-pho gluten guidance notes soy sauce, hoisin and fish sauce commonly used with pho can contain gluten — relevant because this shop's broth uses unspecified 'Vietnamese seasonings' with no wheat-free assurance.
Tabelog lists the restaurant's services as including both allergen accommodations and vegan options.
Restaurant is tagged on Tabelog for allergen accommodation, but the specific scope (which allergens, how requests are handled) was not confirmed from the sources available.
A vegetable-based pho made without meat is offered as a regular menu item, positioned as a lighter option among the 33 pho varieties.

Condiments including chili sauce, herb vinegar and nuoc mam (fish sauce) are set out at the table for diners to add themselves rather than being mixed into dishes beforehand, giving diners some control over fish sauce.

name: plant more（プラント モア） (plant more (Plant More))

claims.text: Plant More advertised gluten-free options, but this primarily applies to desserts, while the meal options are not gluten-free. Some meal items are wheat-free but have a barley mix on top of the salads. Staff confirmed they use the same utensils and bowls to make meal items, so even if they remake a meal there is a high chance of cross contact. The paper menu says to note allergies with your order, but on the website ordering system there is no option to indicate allergies. This establishment is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for those with celiac disease.
Staff are described as lovely and trying to be helpful, but are 'super uninformed with what's actually gluten free and what isn't,' and reviewers recommend avoiding if you're sensitive.
Plant more offers many gluten-free and dairy-free menu items, with staff providing explanations of allergen information for guests.
All desserts (cakes, soft-serve sundaes) are made only with plant-derived ingredients and contain no dairy or eggs.
The menu displays plant-based and allergen markings so that allergy sufferers can order with more confidence.
Listed in WE TABLE's directory of Shinjuku restaurants with food-allergy accommodations.

name: らぁ麺 鳳仙花 (Ra-men Hosenka)

claims.text: The signature broth is a kinmedai/madai fish-bone dashi and the standard topping is pork chashu, so the dish itself is built on fish and meat, not merely at risk of cross-contact.
The shop advertises itself as 無化調 (no added MSG), sourcing its umami from kinmedai/madai bones alone rather than seasoning additives.
